title: Is this the normal way to install packages when building the book?
description:
Hi! I'm new to R and trying to build the book locally to learn offline. When I run `quarto render` after cloning, I keep getting "package not found" errors and have to install them one by one:

1. `quarto render` → "no package called 'tidyverse'"
2. `install.packages("tidyverse")`
3. `quarto render` → "no package called 'nycflights13'" 
4. `install.packages("nycflights13")`
5. Repeat...

This is pretty frustrating as a beginner. Is this how it normally works? 

Would it be possible to add a simple script like `install-deps.R` that installs all needed packages at once? Something like:

```r
# install-deps.R
packages <- c("tidyverse", "nycflights13", "maps", "tidymodels")
for (pkg in packages) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
}
```

Or maybe just list all required packages in the README? 

I'm happy to help make a PR if this would be useful! Just wondering if the current approach is intentional or if there's a better way.

Thanks!

title: Section 12.3, Footnote 2
description:
The footnote reads, "That is, xor(x, y) is true if x is true, or y is true, but not both. This is how we usually use 'or' In English. 'Both' is not usually an acceptable answer to the question 'would you like ice cream or cake?'."

This is incorrect. The inclusive or is used quite frequently, as is the exclusive or. The example given is not actually a terribly good example of the exclusive or: there are many times when someone might want ice cream with their cake! 

Some examples of the inclusive or:

Applicants must have experience in teaching or tutoring.
You can call or text me.
Students can major in mathematics or physics. 
If the flood rises or someone gets hurt, call 911. 

Context is essential to understanding which "or" is meant.

title: Incorrect information regarding Figure 12.1
description:
Hi,

Both in the main text referring to Figure 12.1 and in the caption it is claimed "the complete set of Boolean operations". This is **false**. With two variables x and y there are 4 possible inputs (all combinations of true and false for x and y). For each input there are two possible outputs. This gives 2^4 = 16 possible operators. You only show 7. Some of the 16 operators are less useful than others, but you are missing, for example, the operators NAND, NOR, implication and equivalence. Among the less interesting ones are, for example, the constant true and constant false operators.

The problem is that you are not considering the outside of the two circles. A proper Venn diagram has two circles in a box, with the box denoting the universe. You now have 4 areas corresponding to the 4 possible inputs. Marking these 4 areas you can easily show the 16 different Boolean operations on two variables.

Whether you want to show these 16 operators or not is a matter of taste, but you shouldn't claim that what you have "the complete set".

Best,
Jens

title: Confusing x column in debug output for separate_wider_delim
description:
The ["Strings" chapter](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/strings.html#diagnosing-widening-problems) has an example for debugging widening problems. However, due to the fact that both the original column and one of the output columns are named `x`, the output is a bit confusing:
```R
df <- tibble(x = c("1-1-1", "1-1-2", "1-3", "1-3-2", "1"))

debug <- df |> 
  separate_wider_delim(
    x,
    delim = "-",
    names = c("x", "y", "z"),
    too_few = "debug"
  )
#> Warning: Debug mode activated: adding variables `x_ok`, `x_pieces`, and
#> `x_remainder`.
debug
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   x     y     z     x_ok  x_pieces x_remainder
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr> <lgl>    <int> <chr>      
#> 1 1-1-1 1     1     TRUE         3 ""         
#> 2 1-1-2 1     2     TRUE         3 ""         
#> 3 1-3   3     <NA>  FALSE        2 ""         
#> 4 1-3-2 3     2     TRUE         3 ""         
#> 5 1     <NA>  <NA>  FALSE        1 ""
```

The column `x` still has the original content, and while there are columns for the new `y` and `z` the new `x` column is missing. This can easily be resolved by using a different column name for the original column:
```R
df <- tibble(a = c("1-1-1", "1-1-2", "1-3", "1-3-2", "1"))

debug <- df |> 
  separate_wider_delim(
    a,
    delim = "-",
    names = c("x", "y", "z"),
    too_few = "debug"
  )
#> Warning: Debug mode activated: adding variables `x_ok`, `x_pieces`, and
#> `x_remainder`.
debug
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   x     y       z       a     a_ok  a_pieces a_remainder
#>   <chr> <chr>   <chr>   <chr> <lgl>    <int> <chr>      
#> 1 1     1       1       1-1-1 TRUE         3 ""         
#> 2 1     1       2       1-1-2 TRUE         3 ""         
#> 3 1     3       <NA>    1-3   FALSE        2 ""         
#> 4 1     3       2       1-3-2 TRUE         3 ""         
#> 5 1     <NA>    <NA>    1     FALSE        1 ""
```

I'm happy to create a pull request if you agree that this should be fixed.

title: 12.4.1 on `any()` and `all()`
description:
Section 12.4.1, "Logical summaries", says the following about `any()` and `all()`:

> Like all summary functions, they'll return `NA` if there are any missing values present \[...\].

This doesn't seem right because any instance of `TRUE` or `FALSE`, respectively, will make these functions return non-`NA` values, even if `NA` elements are present. This behavior follows from `any()` and `all()`'s relationship to the binary logical operators, as explained in the same paragraph.

``` r
any(TRUE, NA)
#> [1] TRUE
all(FALSE, NA)
#> [1] FALSE

TRUE | NA
#> [1] TRUE
FALSE & NA
#> [1] FALSE
```

title: Add explanatory images and text for “The rules for missing values in Boolean algebra”
description:
I am a beginner in R and feel that this part is a bit difficult to understand, so I am trying to supplement this part of the content

The rules for missing values in Boolean algebra seem to be attempting to connect circuits

"&" is the extension of another section of the line on the basis of the line, and it is only "True" when the entire line is connected

"|" is to add a line next to the line. If either the original line or the supplementary line is connected, it is "True"

title: When a literal ] appears in square brackets in a regular expression, base R functions find nothing within the range unless perl=TRUE (R for Data Science could mention this)
description:
Section 15.4.3 in R for Data Science (https://r4ds.hadley.nz/regexps.html#character-classes) says this about regular expressions:
`\` escapes special characters, so `[\^\-\]]` matches `^`, `-`, or `]`.
But this specific example does not seem to be true when using base R, unless perl=TRUE is chosen (I am using R 4.2.1).
The general issue of slight differences between base R and stringr is noted in section 15.7.2, but perhaps this particular quirk is worth mentioning in 15.4.3 as the example contains one of these differences.

For example:
```grepl("[\\^\\-\\]]", "]")```
returns FALSE. 
And:
```grepl("[\\^\\-\\]]", "^-]")```
also returns FALSE, indicating that nothing in the range is found in the string.
But only the ] symbol appears to cause this. So:
```grepl("[\\^\\-\\[]", "^-]")```
returns TRUE, seemingly because the ] is not there (in this example it has been replaced by [ but it could just as well be replaced by nothing).

This issue seems to go away entirely when perl=TRUE is used, so:
```grepl("[\\^\\-\\]]", "]", perl=TRUE)```
and
```grepl("[\\^\\-\\]]", "-", perl=TRUE)```
both return TRUE.

Perhaps there could to be a note in the book to reflect this, or perhaps it is an issue with base R or the TRE engine.

title: Issue with make_datetime_100
description:
The make_datetime_100 function in the lubridate chapter does not seem to be entirely accurate. The timezone information is neglected while using the make_datetime function and this leads to the default timezone (UTC) being adopted for all datetimes created using this function. This is not a problem for the examples thereafter, but if one were to compare datetimes from different timezones, especially by using the arr_time and the sched_arr_time, the results would not be correct.

For example, if we were to print the arrival time of all flights according to the departure time zone, using something like the following

``` r
flights_dt %>% 
  mutate(arr_time_in_deptz = with_tz(arr_time, dep_time %>% tz())) 
```

, it would not give the exepected results as the timezones all match in the first place, they are all UTC.

Similarly, if we were to create graphs based on the arrival times rather than the departure times as shown in the examples, one needs to be very careful about the interpretation, as the destinations are all in different timezones. This could also be explained, or simply, the creation of the arr_time and the sched_arr_time removed from the flights_dt data frame to avoid incorrect usage.

The accurate solution is perhaps to join the flights with the airports table which has a timezone column. 

``` r
# use the timezone as string info. Note: a group_by(timezone) is needed with with_tz when using this function. This is because with_tz is not vectorised.
make_datetime_100_tzone <- function(year, month, day, time, timezone) {
  make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100, tz = timezone)
}

# create a function for composing the date and time when the time zone offset is known
make_datetime_100_tz <- function(year, month, day, time, tzoffset) {
  make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100) + hours(tzoffset)
}
```

Again, this is not really straightforward, as there are limitations to using this in further examples involving the time zone. A problem is while trying to use with_tz later on this datetime; as with_tz is not vectorised, results will not be as expected. (group_by, rowwise or purr seem to be workarounds). Perhaps it is simply better to omit the arrival times from the flights_dt data frame and keep the examples simple, until support for timezones is improved.

Thanks for your attention!
KS

title: dplyr::group_nest() is advised in Iteration chapter, but may become deprecated
description:
In the Iteration chapter, `dplyr::group_nest()` is advised in order to restructure a data frame in such a way that rows represent the unique combinations of grouping variables and the remaining variables are moved to a list column (list of tibbles).

However the documentation of `dplyr::group_nest()` currently states:

> `group_nest()` is not stable because `tidyr::nest(.by =)` provides very similar behavior. It may be deprecated in the future.

So I'd suggest to indeed use `nest(.by =)` (or `group_by() |> nest()`). I could make a pull request to implement that if you like.

title: implicit vs. explicit
description:
Hi there, I was reading the section on tidy data just now and I think it's a great workup of both concept and package. 

The only thing that I think you might want to change is the sentence

> An implicit missing value is the presence of an absence; an explicit missing value is the absence of a presence.

where explicit and implicit should trade places.

As a reference, I think the book for ggplot2 got it right where it says:

> An `NA` is the presence of an absence; but sometimes a missing value is the absence of a presence.

Finally, a big thanks for writing this book, it's got a great deal of refreshing clarity. 
Best,
David Wolski

title: Ordered factors
description:
This line
https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/main/factors.qmd#L416
says that ordered factors  " equal distance between levels"  but that is not the case, if they were equidistant that would be interval and could be represented by a number.  What makes them distinct is that while ordered there is no underlying common unit of measurement.  E.g. Strongly agree could be a lot farther from Agree than Agree is from neutral.

Also it has two periods at the end.

title: mutate() function not accepting .before=/.after= arguments
description:
Trying to reproduce examples from the book 'R for Data Science' (2nd ed), chapter 'Data Transformation', section headed 'mutate()'

```r
# Windows 7 pro 64bit, Service Pack 1
# RStudio version 1.3.1093
# R.Version()   -> # 4.3.1

library(nycflights13)

nycflights13::flights

flights |> 
  mutate(
    gain = dep_delay - arr_delay,
    speed = distance / air_time * 60
  )
flights |> 
  mutate(
    gain = dep_delay - arr_delay,
    speed = distance / air_time * 60,
    .before = 1
  )
flights |> 
  mutate(
    gain = dep_delay - arr_delay,
    speed = distance / air_time * 60,
    .after = day
  )
```

The two new columns gain & speed are invariably added to the right end, despite the arguments .before=1 and .after=day in the latter two calls, contrary to the examples presented in the book.
Rather, the arguments are interpreted as new variables to be created, named .before resp. .after, and coded <dbl> 1 invariably.
By contrast, the arguments .before/.after worked well when I used them in relocate() functions, as suggested by their use of "tidy selection, as opposed to "data masking" used by mutate() [see <https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/programming.html>, which I might have to read five more times in order to perhaps know what to do :) ].
=> Why does my R not reproduce the results presented in the book, despite using the identical code?

title: separate_wider_regex example doesn't match style guide?
description:
On [the Regex page](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/regexps), there's this example:

```
df |> 
  [separate_wider_regex](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/separate_wider_delim.html)(
    str,
    patterns = [c](https://rdrr.io/r/base/c.html)(
      "<", 
      name = "[A-Za-z]+", 
      ">-", 
      gender = ".", "_", 
      age = "[0-9]+"
    )
  )
```

When reading it, I was temporarily confused by the `gender` argument. I thought it was some kind of array of two characters. But actually `"_"` is a second argument, not part of gender.

Why is it on the same line as gender, when the other string literals (`"<"`) are on their own line?

Should this be

```
df |>

      age = "[0-9]+"

Normally I wouldn't be so pedantic about style. But since this is a guide for beginners, perhaps style is important.

title: quote package names in all `library()` calls throughout the book
description:
I keep coming back to this question in various contexts and finally did a cursory search for this question, prompted by non-quoted package names in this R book:

Wouldn't be a good default to *always* quote the package name in `library()` calls, to avoid unexpected side-effects where variable names identical to a package name exist?

There is a nice [question and answer regarding package name quotation on Stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/a/36803188/2352071), which basically gives two reasons to always quote package names. Namely:

1. [The Journal of Statistical Software requires this in its "style guide"](https://www.jstatsoft.org/style#miscellaneous).
2. [Hadley's **Advanced R** book names exactly the above mentioned problem with variable names identical to package names as a downside of non-standard evaluation](http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Computing-on-the-language.html#nse-downsides).

Most important for me in this context is the reasoning behind `2.`, so I'll copy the example here (with a bit more context):

For a plain R environment, I get the following attached packages with `sessionInfo()`:
```
R version 4.3.0 (2023-04-21)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
Running under: CentOS Linux 7 (Core

[...]

attached base packages:
[1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base
[...]
```

I then run the example from the above link under `2.`, namely:
```
ggplot2 <- "plyr"
library(ggplot2)
```

If I then rerun `sessionInfo()`, I get these attached packages:
```
[...]

attached base packages:
[1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base     

other attached packages:
[1] ggplot2_3.4.1

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
 [1] utf8_1.2.3       R6_2.5.1         tidyselect_1.2.0 magrittr_2.0.3   gtable_0.3.1     glue_1.6.2       tibble_3.1.8     pkgconfig_2.0.3 
 [9] generics_0.1.3   dplyr_1.1.0      lifecycle_1.0.3  cli_3.6.0        fansi_1.0.4      scales_1.2.1     grid_4.3.0       vctrs_0.5.2     
[17] withr_2.5.0      compiler_4.3.0   rstudioapi_0.14  tools_4.3.0      munsell_0.5.0    pillar_1.8.1     colorspace_2.1-0 rlang_1.0.6
```

So the default seems to guard against the worst, which would be to have the `ggplot2 <- "plyr"` result in loading the `"plyr"` package with the command `library(ggplot2)`. But for being consistent and avoid confusing newcomers (and regularly bugging more experienced R users;), I would suggest to:

* [ ] Consistently quote the first argument in calls like `library("ggplot2")` throughout the book.
* [ ] Maybe do the same for the [other functions that have non-standard evaluation of arguments](http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Computing-on-the-language.html#nse-downsides).
* [ ] Reference the respective section of **Advanced R** somewhere (unless I just missed such a mention so far).

I'm glad to chip in with a PR here, but figured I'd first ask if not quoting package names was maybe some conscious choice with a good reason behind it.

title: "+ve" and "-ve" may be confusing to non-native speakers of English

In [Logical Vectors > Conditional Transformations](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/logicals.html#conditional-transformations), `if_else()` is introduced by using it to classify numbers to be either positive or negative. The shorthands "+ve" and "-ve" are used to this end: "Let’s begin with a simple example of labeling a numeric vector as either '+ve' or '-ve'". 

In my experience, "+ve" and "-ve" are not well known by non-native speakers of English (including myself as of about 15 years ago). I suggest simply using "positive" and "negative" instead to avoid confusion (or "pos" / "neg" if the result should be short).

title: Chapter 6, example on how pivoting works
description:
Thank you very much for this outstanding book!

While explaining the concept of tidy data using R4DS (2e), I was a bit confused by the example in 6.3.2. Doesn't the tibble contain the same "problem" as  6.3.4 ("Data and variable names in the header"), because "bp" is a variable (name) and the digits are the values for the variable "measurement". According to 6.3.4, shouldn't the tibble be better pivoted like this?

``` r
# Create tibble
df <- tribble(
  ~id,  ~bp1, ~bp2,
  "A",  100,  120,
  "B",  140,  115,
  "C",  120,  125
)

# Make tibble tidy
df |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = bp1:bp2,
    names_to = c(".value", "measurement"),
    names_pattern = "(..)(.)"
  ) 
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   id    measurement    bp
#>   <chr> <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 A     1             100
#> 2 A     2             120
#> 3 B     1             140
#> 4 B     2             115
#> 5 C     1             120
#> 6 C     2             125
``` 

Maybe the tibble in the example could just get different column names to begin with to get around this issue?

``` r
# Create tibble
df <- tribble(
  ~id,  ~m1, ~m2,
  "A",  100,  120,
  "B",  140,  115,
  "C",  120,  125
)

# Make tibble tidy
df |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !id,
    names_to = "measurement",
    values_to = "value"
  ) 
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   id    measurement  value
#>   <chr> <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 A     m1            100
#> 2 A     m2            120
#> 3 B     m1            140
#> 4 B     m2            115
#> 5 C     m1            120
#> 6 C     m2            125
```
In addition, a column name in Figures 6.3, 6.4, and 6.5 does not match the tidied tibble ("measurement" vs. "name").

title: Ch6 comments
description:
### easy fixes
I really like the `billboard` addition! It is much more elegant than the old WHO example. A few easy suggestions:
- [ ] It’s confusing that it says the year 2000 but then has data from 76 weeks when there are only 52 weeks in a year! The answer is that the dataset includes all weeks from any song which **ever** appeared in `billboard` in 2000. This is a nice implied lesson about how it’s hard to draw time boundaries in panel data. Whether or not you point that out, useful to at least clarify dataset definition.

There’s a few math steps that I think will be clarifying to students for thinking about data structure. 
- [ ] First, the dataset starts with 317 rows and 76 weeks. So pivot_longer generates a data frame with 317*76 = 24,092 rows. 
- [ ] Second, the number of rows falls dramatically (by 78%) with `values_drop_na = TRUE`. So this isn’t just affecting 2Pac, it’s affecting a huge swath of the dataset. Both of these points implicit in the current code output and might be obvious to you, but won’t be to a reader unless we draw it out.

### more time-consuming bigger issues
- [ ]  A key part of dataset cleaning is bringing to bear your intuitive knowledge about what’s true. This song list may be unfamiliar to someone who is 30 or under. Can you pull a more recent year?
- [ ] As a reader, I struggled with the `cms_patient_experience` example for `pivot_wider()`. Unlike the `billboard` example, it’s not clear at all what the endgame is for this dataset so it’s not clear why the current structure is suboptimal and the proposed structure is superior. Going even further, if you wanted to do some analysis in ggplot (e.g. ratings over time, if we had more than one rating per institution), the original structure is superior. At the very least, I would clarify why we want `pivot_wider()` here. I think maybe the wider version is more readable? Alternatively, if you’re open to using a different example, feel free to assign this back to me and I’ll try to come up with something, understanding that it might not make the cut because the book is closing on March 7.

description:
_I have taught the past four years using 1e to students with close to no background in coding, which has been a  good reminder of just how hard it is to learn and how the smallest details in console output can be quite confusing to someone starting out. I have not, as of yet, committed any solutions via PRs. I’m happy to do so in the cases where you think that I am on the right track with my concerns. Through off-github correspondence with Hadley, we converged on the idea of posting one issue per chapter._

Teaching `geom_bar()` in conjunction with `fill` is **really** confusing to students, especially with `position = “fill”`. I can’t give a deep explanation of why, although I think it’s related to the facts that (a) there’s no variable named “fill” and (b) they never see the intermediate output with the relative frequency count. I think you’ll probably serve your readers best by dropping this example at this point in the text. If you keep it, the following code block would be sufficient to generate the intermediate output, but I note that grouped mutate doesn’t appear until _much_ later in the textbook.
```
penguins |>
    count(island, species) |>
    group_by(island) |>
    mutate(share = n/sum(n))
```
Another alternative would be to move up Figure 11.2, add some “share” columns, and that way you wouldn’t need to explain the verbs to calculate it.

title: Comments, chapter uncertain
description:
### loss of grouped mutate & filter
- [ ] In chapter 15, I’m surprised that grouped `mutate()` and `filter()` gets so little air time given that it is incredibly useful in the real-world. 1e has useful [examples](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/transform.html#grouped-mutates-and-filters). I found that the examples were too brief to be clear for my students and over the years my slides evolved into 
[grouped mutate and filter slides.pdf](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/files/10854387/grouped.mutate.and.filter.slides.pdf). I think it is quite important to explain grouped `mutate()` and `filter()`. Could be Ch 15, but could be elsewhere.

### writing tests
- [ ] I think it would be very useful to teach students to explicitly write tests, rather than simply printing material to the console where the analyst verifies by inspection that the claim is true. 

For example, after the print statements in 21.2.2, one could include: 
```
test_that(
  "There are no tailnums that appear more than once",
  expect_equal(
    planes %>%
    count(tailnum) %>%
    filter(n > 1) %>%
    nrow(),
    0
) ) 
```
I also suggest a function which is effectively a test in Chapter 27 https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/issues/1327

### cross-cutting bug
- [ ] Avoid ever numbering data frames (e.g. `flights2`). This is just teaching students bad hygiene (and further [seems](https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#object-names) inconsistent with the style guide). Either stick with the name `flights` or name it `flights_what_i_did`

title: Ch4 comments
description:
### 4.4.2 
- [ ] I recommend moving the material on counts from Section 15.3 up to here. This is where I teach `count()`. Why? it’s much more intuitive to a student who is starting out to say “count the number of flights each month” than it is to say “group_by(month) %>% summarize(n = n())”. Why not teach the intuitive syntax first and then show how if you want to compute both the mean and n() simultaneously you can do both via the `group_by()` syntax? 

- [ ] Small pedantic point: it is pretty confusing that 
```
flights |> 
  group_by(month) |> 
  summarize(
    delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE), 
    n = n()
  )
``` 
reports n() inclusive of NA values but delay stats exclusive of NA values. I don’t have an easy fix for the text here, I’m just noting an issue.

### 4.4.3
- [ ] `slice_max` output and the `summarize` output are actually not symmetric! `slice_max` reports two rows each for `CHS`, `ILM` and `RSW` for a total of 118 rows.
	Options: (a) lean into the differences in output and explain them OR (b) switch to using `dep_delay` which reports 115 rows for both verbs. (Personally, as a teacher, I feel like this is a great example to lean into to show how the two functions work slightly different, but this may be too subtle or make the book longer than you would like.)

- [ ] Warnings really throw students off! Why is the code giving me a warning? Did I do something wrong?
	Options: (a) explain that the warning arises because there’s one (likely errant) flight from EWR to LGA, (b) filter out this pesky flight, OR (c) change the example to use say first instead of max. (Again, I would probably lean into the errant row, but I realize you are trying to close the book)

### 4.5
- [ ] remove superfluous `na.rm = TRUE`

title: Tiny fixes: Chs 11, 13, 15, 21, 28
description:
### Chapter 11
- [ ] Delete “(You’ll learn how `filter()` works in the chapter on data transformations: for now, just know that this command selects only the subcompact cars.)”. This is presumably a legacy from when layers were explained before filter().

### Chapter 13
- [ ] It can be very useful for students to revisit old ideas with new tools. Ch 11 has a very nice example of using red open circle to highlight that two-seater cars deviate from the general fuel efficiency trend. In 13.3 where you teach annotation, it would be great to revisit this. For example, you could re-up the old plot with the added annotation 
> In general, increasing engine size is \nrelated to decreasing fuel economy… *but two-seaters cars achieve superior fuel economy in spite of their large engines*

where the italicized part is the new idea

### Chapter 15.6.3 & 15.6.7 
- [ ] The airport `EGE` did not move. You can easily see this by running
`flights %>% filter(dest == "EGE") %>% count(origin, carrier, distance)`
Rather, the issue is that almost everything in this dataset is reported by the airlines and United and American have slightly different recorded distances for this flight. I suggest using `IQR(distance)` and then using the `count()` verb to uncover the bug. Alternately, come up with a different IQR example (or I can).

### Chapter 21
- [ ] I can’t figure out the answer to 
> What do the tail numbers that don’t have a matching record in planes have in common? (Hint: one variable explains ~90% of the problems.) 

My solution algorithm was to use 
`flights %>% select(-year) %>% anti_join(planes) %>% count(varname)` 
and then permute over all of the variable names.

It's possible that others will find this question difficult and that a rewrite or different hint is in order

### Chapter 28.2.2
> “It’s important to note that we’re passing this function to [across()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html), so [across()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html) can call it, not calling it ourselves.” 

Sounds grammatically awkward even if it is correct. Better might be 
—“It’s important to note that we’re passing this function to [across()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html), so [across()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html) can call it, ~not~ **rather than** calling it ourselves.” 
—“It’s important to note that we’re passing this function to [across()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html), so [across()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html) can call it ~,~ **;** we’re not calling it ourselves.”

title: Ch27 comments
description:
There are two ways in principle that one might teach function writing: 
1. You already have written mostly repetitive code A & B and now you need to find the shared element and write a third version of the code C where the function is used to abstract from the repetitive parts 
2. You have written a hack-y version of some analysis for one case. Now you want to prepare it for repeated use across the codebase.

The textbook only teaches version (1), but in my life as a data analyst, I find that (2) is a much more common use case. It might therefore make sense to have an example which shows (2). I suggest one example below, but I am very glad to iterate and search for other examples if this overall way of framing seems helpful to you. 

Manual version for one case
```
planes %>% nrow() == planes %>% distinct(tailnum) %>% nrow()
test_that("tailnum primary?", expect_equal(n_row, n_tails))
```

Functionalized version
```
check_unique <- function(df, candidate_var) {
  n_row <- df %>% nrow()
  n_candidate_var <- df %>% distinct({{ candidate_var }}) %>% nrow()
  n_row == n_candidate_var 
}
check_unique(planes, tailnum)
check_unique(planes, manufacturer)
```

Remarks:
*  I note that my example requires embracing and so it wouldn’t work in its current form where the other “how to write” examples are, but I’m sure I can come up with something else that would fit.
* there’s an example in the spirit of what I’m suggesting in 28.3.6, but that’s not an area where we are teaching how to write functions

title: OK to use material for accompanying tutorials
description:
I would like to use the material in R4DS to create some accompanying tutorials. Any objections?

Background:

1) The license for R4DS is "Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0". The NoDerivs part can be tricky.

2) I write [lots of tutorials](https://github.com/PPBDS/all.primer.tutorials) for my students. See [here](https://ppbds.github.io/all.primer.tutorials/articles/instructions.html) for details on my approach.

3) I would like to, for example, create a tutorial about web scraping which would cajole/force students to type all the commands in the web scraping [chapter](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/webscraping.html). To do that, I would (obviously) need to use the same code/example as in the chapter itself.

If the license were simply "Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial", then there would be no worries. But the NoDerivs part makes it unclear whether I need permission. So, I thought I would at least ask.

Big fan of the first and second editions!

title: Adding explanation of `dep_time` of `flights` dataset
description:
### Problem 

We can add an explanation for the last chunk of <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-style.html#spaces> but I am not sure to add the data explanation in this *code style* chapter.

   ```
   flights |> 
     mutate(
       speed      = air_time / distance,
       dep_hour   = dep_time %/% 100,
       dep_minute = dep_time %%  100
     )
   ```

---

### Reasons

1. We use `%/%` and `%%` first time in [7.2 Spaces](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-style.html#spaces) and [12.4 Unusual values](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/eda#sec-unusual-values-eda) but we explain these operators in [15.4.3 Modular arithmetic](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/numbers.html#modular-arithmetic).
2. 
   Even though it is mentioned in the documentation below and also recommended at <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#nycflights13>, we might still briefly mention `dep_time` is in `HMM` or `HHMM` format in the plaintext because I think it feels like typo that we need to replace `100` by `60` at first glance.
   ```
   library(nycflights13)
   ?flights
   ```

---

### Possible Explanation

``
Since `dep_time` is in HMM or HHMM fomat, we use integer division (`%/%`) to get hour and remainder (`%%`) to get minute.
``

title: Exercise 4.3.5 1. Problems
description:

> (Compare air_time with arr_time - dep_time. What do you expect to see? What do you see? What do you need to do to fix it? 

is very frustrating for new(-ish) R users, because in the context of the exercise, the `air_time` in the `flights` data set is a misleading variable. `air_time`  is  purely the time spent in the air, which cannot be achieved by manipulating `dep_time` and `arr_time` in any way (as suggested in the exercise). To make `arr_time - dep_time` be the same as `air_time`, one cannot simply convert the HHMM format to minutes, because the resulting values are still off, since both `dep_time` and `arr_time` include not only the time spent in the air, but also the time spent on the runway.

title: Notes on the spreadsheets chapter
description:
Chapter looks great! I just made a few observations here, but definitely don't necessarily think they all need to be acted on. Take what's useful and ignore the rest.

> xlsx and XLConnect can also be used for reading data from and writing data to Excel spreadsheets.

I think openxlsx is actually the 2nd most used "excel-handling" package, after readxl so I would sort of expect to see it here. (Ecosystem-wise, I think it's also important re: writing rich spreadsheets, but maybe you don't get into that. Update: I now see that you do. So maybe just mention openxlsx here and say it'll come up later.)

> The column names are all over the place.

Presumably you considered this, but providing a function (like `janitor::clean_names()`) might be worth a mention as something that scales better than hard-wiring actual names.

> By default, only "" (empty string, or, in the case of reading from a spreadsheet, an empty cell) is recognized as an NA.

Technically that's not true. True "spreadsheet NAs" are also read as `NA`. For example, if a cell has the formula `=NA()`, which displays as `#N/A`, it gets read as `NA`. But I could understand if you don't want to get into that.

> The syntax is a bit different, though.

Re: col type specification. This is such a nice way of saying "the syntax is much more awkward" :disappointed_relieved:

> It took us multiple steps and trial-and-error to load the data in exactly the format we want, and this is not unexpected. Data science is an iterative process. 

I think spreadsheets, in particular, tend to be very weird and dirty because humans have usually interacted with them, with their bare and unwashed hands.

> That might be tempting, but it’s strongly not recommended as Excel can modify certain types of data upon launch with no way to track this change.

I feel like this is too much FUD and it's too discouraging re: looking at the actual data. Presumably you've already got an `.xlsx` file, so opening it, in most cases is relatively low risk. The genes as dates problem occurs more when data is first going into a spreadsheet. I.e. if you've already got an `.xlsx` that you need to read, it's rare that opening it in Excel is going to make things *worse*. (There *are* some things where Excel changes what's on disk when you merely open a file, but I wouldn't dwell on that too much.)

I also think it's just impractical to think that people aren't going to open an Excel file in Excel. It's like "just say no".

> Reading individual sheets

I would say "worksheet" here and lots of other places. But you're probably saying "sheet" because the argument is `sheet`.

> `read_excel(deaths_path, range = cell_limits(c(5, 1), c(15, 6)))`

I'm not sure `cell_limits()` is worth showing. It's mostly useful internally and mostly because it allows for partially open rectangles. I guess if you decide to show it, that would be the thing to mention? But I'd probably suppress it.

> A cell can be one of five things ... A currency

This seems odd to me and it's really not true. There isn't such a cell type and I would leave it off, for parallelism. It's just like a date time, where the underlying cell type is numeric and then the display is controlled by a format. Another example would be a percentage. Or even a number where we including comma as the grouping mark (between the thousands) or parentheses to indicate a negative number.

> These differences between how the underlying data are stored vs. how they’re displayed can cause surprises when the data are loaded into R.

This is a VERY important point. What you see (in Excel) is NOT what's on disk.

> You can do this with `gs4_auth()` ...

Perhaps worth pointing out that you can sit back and let googlesheets4 prompt you for auth. You only need to call `gs4_auth()` explicitly if you have some non-default goals (like specifying the email or whatnot).

title: Find home for making groups
description:
Before we move on to the next chapter, we want to show you one last trick that's useful for grouping data.
Sometimes you want to start a new group every time some event occurs.
For example, when you're looking at website data, it's common to want to break up events into sessions, where a session is defined as a gap of more than x minutes since the last activity.

Here's some made up data that illustrates the problem.
So far computed the time lag between the events, and figured out if there's a gap that's big enough to qualify:

```{r}
events <- tibble(
  time = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 12, 15, 17, 19, 20, 27, 28, 30)
)
events <- events |> 
  mutate(
    diff = time - lag(time, default = first(time)),
    gap = diff >= 5
  )
events
```

But how do we go from that logical vector to something that we can `group_by()`?
`consecutive_id()` comes to the rescue:

```{r}
events |> mutate(
  group = consecutive_id(gap)
)
```

`consecutive_id()` starts a new group every time one of its arguments changes.
That makes it useful both here, with logical vectors, and in many other place.
For example, inspired by [this stackoverflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27482712), imagine you have a data frame with a bunch of repeated values:

```{r}
df <- tibble(
  x = c("a", "a", "a", "b", "c", "c", "d", "e", "a", "a", "b", "b"),
  y = c(1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 1, 3, 9, 4, 8, 10, 199)
)
df
```

You want to keep the first row from each repeated `x`.
That's easier to express with a combination of `consecutive_id()` and `slice_head()`:

```{r}
df |> 
  group_by(id = consecutive_id(x)) |> 
  slice_head(n = 1)
```

description:
Hi @mine-cetinkaya-rundel! I'm responding to your call for feedback on the quarto chapter. These are minor. I think the chapter is great! I particularly liked the additions to the YAML header section 😄 

Now, for my comments:

- [x] Though I think this ordering was intentional, the section on the _source editor_ still reads as if it should come before the one from the _visual editor_. Mostly, I think this is because the visual editor section mentions [Pandoc markdown](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/9bba5cb695105d95f427cba306e98cde0eb11979/quarto.qmd#L146), but it's the [next section](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/9bba5cb695105d95f427cba306e98cde0eb11979/quarto.qmd#L182-L185) that explains what it is.
- [x] The _caching_ section seems a bit out-of-place. In terms of logical order, I think global options and inline code are more common, but presented later. I see you are moving _Figures_ and _Tables_ up in the document hierarchy (from an H3 to an H2 heading), so perhaps the same would make sense for caching.
- [x] It could be worth a mention that one common source of rendering errors can come from repeating the same label in different chunks. You could add this either in the "chunk label" or "troubleshooting" sections, or as an exercise (I think the certified RStudio trainers test had something like this).
- [x] Some of the examples in the chapter [use underscores in the chunk labels](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/9bba5cb695105d95f427cba306e98cde0eb11979/quarto.qmd#L408) instead of the [suggested dashes](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/9bba5cb695105d95f427cba306e98cde0eb11979/quarto.qmd#L274-L275). I think the motivation behind this suggestion [was this hard-to-debug issue when generating PDFs](https://yihui.org/en/2018/03/space-pain/). 
- [x] [The qmd example at the beginning of the chapter](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/9bba5cb695105d95f427cba306e98cde0eb11979/quarto.qmd#L50-L62) doesn't have any text formatting, unlike what is mentioned in the third bullet-point in the text right below.
- [x] A couple of places still use _knit_ instead of _render_.
- [x] This [cross-reference](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/9bba5cb695105d95f427cba306e98cde0eb11979/quarto.qmd#L353) should be to the _Figures_ section in the same document.

I hope these are helpful, and congrats on this new edition! It's shaping up very nicely.

title: Ambiguity in section 21.4.1 Ex. 1
description:
The question reads:

> Read the documentation for `apply()`. In the 2d case, what two for loops does it generalize?

The first time, I read "2d case" as the "2nd case", which may owe as much to me spending too much time reading historical works where 2d and 3d were abbreviations for 2nd and 3rd as it does to reading too fast. But the documentation of `apply()` has two paragraphs on what it does when `FUN` returns vectors of the same size, and what it does when `FUN` returns vectors of different sizes.  I suggest using "2-d", or making 2-dimensions more explicit.

I don't know if `apply()` "generalizes" for loops. I think of it more as a replacement.

I think something like the following may be a more clear question that accomplishes the same intent.

> Read the documentation for `apply()`. Rewrite the `apply()` calls using for loops.
> ```r
> df <- tibble(
>   a = rnorm(10),
>   b = rnorm(10),
>   c = rnorm(10),
>   d = rnorm(10)
> )
> apply(df, 1, mean)
> apply(df, 2, mean)
> apply(df, c(1, 2), mean)
```

title: Problems with Exercise 21.5.3
description:
The question text is:

> Rewrite map(x, function(df) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = df)) to eliminate the anonymous function.

The code is confusing. What is this code supposed to represent?  What is `x`? It must be a list of data frames, given the function. mpg %>%
  split(.$cyl)
  map(x, function(df) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = df))
```
Although an example in the chapter already splits by `cyl` and gives this answer. Perhaps `mtcars` could be split by `vs` or `am`? 

Alternatively, replace the question with another

Second, by removing the anonymous function, do you mean to use the shortcut one-sided formula, or actually write a named function. To me, the later is simply syntactic sugar in purrr for creating a one-sided function.

title: Suggestion: replace `pwalk(list(...), ...)` by `walk2(..., ...)` in iteration chapter
description:
Current code:
```
library(ggplot2)
plots <- mtcars %>% 
  split(.$cyl) %>% 
  map(~ggplot(., aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point())
paths <- stringr::str_c(names(plots), ".pdf")

pwalk(list(paths, plots), ggsave, path = tempdir())
```
Suggestion (watch the last line):
```
library(ggplot2)
plots <- mtcars %>% 
  split(.$cyl) %>% 
  map(~ggplot(., aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point())
paths <- stringr::str_c(names(plots), ".pdf")

walk2(paths, plots, ggsave, path = tempdir())
```
Rationale:
- simpler code
- no reason to use `pwalk()` while there are only 2 lists

Note:

I submitted PR #668 with typos corrections and I push to it whenever I find new typos. If you agreed with this change, I could push it to that PR as well.

title: Primary key of `nycflights13::flights` and `nycflights13::weather`
description:
## Primary key of `flights`

In the chapter on Relational Data, section [Keys](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/relational-data.html#keys), the text describes the `flights` table as having no primary key.

> Sometimes a table doesn’t have an explicit primary key: each row is an observation, but no combination of variables reliably identifies it. For example, what’s the primary key in the flights table? You might think it would be the date plus the flight or tail number, but neither of those are unique:

However, (`year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, `carrier`, `flight`) is a primary key.

``` r
library("tidyverse")
library("nycflights")
#> Error in library("nycflights"): there is no package called 'nycflights'

flights %>% 
  count(year, month, day, hour, carrier, flight) %>% 
  filter(n > 1)
#> Error in eval(lhs, parent, parent): object 'flights' not found
```
<sup>Created on 2019-01-19 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

## Primary key of `weather`

The text mentions (`year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, `origin`) as possibly being a primary key for weather but shows in the code that it is not. However, there is no discussion in prose of this failure. Are the duplicated observations intentional?

```r
weather %>% 
  count(year, month, day, hour, origin) %>% 
  filter(n > 1)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>    year month   day  hour origin     n
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int> <chr>  <int>
#> 1  2013    11     3     1 EWR        2
#> 2  2013    11     3     1 JFK        2
#> 3  2013    11     3     1 LGA        2
```

## Problems with nycflights database diagam

In either, case the relational diagram is incorrect:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/123968/51434283-16dbbf80-1c12-11e9-85cc-b0fa57d9db2f.png) 

-  In `flights`, the gray shading indicates that (`year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`,  `flight`) is a primary key, which it is not. The combination of (`year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`,  `flight`, `carrier`) would work.
-  In `weather`, the gray shading of (`year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, `origin`)
 indicates that it is a primary key, which it is not; with the counterexamples given earlier.

I'm not sure about the relationship between `flights` and `weather`.  The arrows indicate that (`year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, `origin`) of `flights` is a foreign key of `weather`.  However, for that relation to hold - those columns need to be a primary key of `flights` and all values in `weather` should have a `match` in flights. Neither of those are true. There are many hours in `weather` that don't have any flights.

``` r
library("tidyverse")
library("nycflights13")

anti_join(weather, flights,
          by = c("year", "month", "day", "hour", "origin")) %>%
  nrow()
#> [1] 6737
```

I maybe totally wrong on all this though. You may be using a looser definition of these, or another form of relation.

title: feedback on "Data rectangling" chapter
description:
Hi, I've seen [a tweet](https://twitter.com/hadleywickham/status/1544470643047006208) from @hadley mentioning this chapter and I gave it a read, as it would have helped me a lot in my past year of fighting with json objects 😄 

To be honest I have more questions than feedback, mostly related to my experience with rectangling, but I hope they might still be helpful.

### Performance of  `unnest_*` functions vs `map_*`
Is there any difference between using `unnest_wider` and then `select`ing the columns that I need, versus using a series of `map_*` calls to extract directly the things that I need? 
My code was really slow, I tried this to make things faster and it worked, but I changed more than one thing at a time, so I'm not sure if this actually makes any difference.

### Handling `NULL` values with `map_*`
Using `map_*` variants to extract information with a vector of names gave me a new problem, missing elements in the lists were returning `NULL` and the `map_*` variants give an error. 
It took me a while to discover the `.default` argument, which solves most of my issues, my previous solution was to extract with `map` and then coercing the result with `as.*` functions. 

Since this was so hard to discover/solve, I fear that I might be using a suboptimal (if not off label) strategy. And if it's not suboptimal I think that `.default` deserves a bit more exposure 😅 

### Usage of `hoist`
I've seen `hoist` mentioned a couple of times in the past but I've never really understood how it works. The example in the chapter is the first time that I understand it a bit more, but it's still quite obscure.  

Could I use it instead of the series of `map_*` calls?
This is an example of what I do now to make a table from a `jsonlite` list, in this case each element is in the first level, but there are cases where I pass a vector of names for nested elements.

```
info_sessioni<-tibble::tibble(
    ss_id = purrr::map_chr(sessions_l, "id"),
    subject_id = purrr::map_chr(sessions_l,"subject_id", .default = NA_character_),
    n_answers = purrr::map_int(sessions_l, "n_answers", .default = NA_integer_),
    started_on = purrr::map_chr(sessions_l, "started_on", .default = NA_character_),
    last_action = purrr::map_chr(sessions_l, "last_action", .default = NA_character_),
    completed_on = purrr::map_chr(sessions_l, "completed_on", .default = NA_character_),
    params_data = purrr::map_chr(sessions_l, "data", .default = "{}"),
    user_agent = purrr::map_chr(sessions_l, "user_agent",.default = NA_character_)
  )
```



I see that a bunch of new chapters are about topics that I learned recently about on my own.
I understand that it's not exactly the feedback on the contents that you were looking for, but if this kind of feedback is useful in any way I can open other issues, since I'll be reading the new chapters anyway 😄

title: Durations for dyears typo
description:
In Section 16.4.1 it is written: 

"Durations always record the time span in seconds. Larger units are created by converting minutes, hours, days, weeks, and years to seconds at the standard rate (60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in day, 7 days in a week, 365 days in a year)."

However, the years are not converted at the standard rate (365) for `dyears()`, but at the rate of 365.25. This also affects an example later in Section 16.4.2:

```
  # A leap year
  ymd("2016-01-01") + dyears(1)
  #> [1] "2016-12-31 06:00:00 UTC"
  ymd("2016-01-01") + years(1)
  #> [1] "2017-01-01"
```

where the difference is not only due to a leap year but also due to `dyears()` using 365.25. For example `ymd("2016-01-01") + dhours(24 * 365)` returns `"2016-12-31"`

title: 15.4 explain what `x` and `y` is for `fct_reorder2()`
description:
For `fct_reorder()`

> `fct_reorder()` takes three arguments:

> * `f`, the factor whose levels you want to modify.
> * `x`, a numeric vector that you want to use to reorder the levels.
> * Optionally, `fun`, a function that's used if there are multiple values of
  `x` for each value of `f`. The default value is `median`.

So it's clear that in

```r
ggplot(relig_summary, aes(tvhours, fct_reorder(relig, tvhours))) +
  geom_point()
```
`relig` is `f`, `tvhours` is `x`.

title: unnest() no longer fails when attempting to unnest list-columns of different lengths
description:
The [last example](https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/master/model-many.Rmd#L545-L552) in the "Many models" chapter no longer fails because `unnest()` recycles the shorter elements from the list-columns:

```r
# Doesn't work because y and z have different number of elements
df2 <- tribble(
  ~x, ~y,           ~z,
   1, "a",         1:2,  
   2, c("b", "c"),   3
)
df2
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>       x y         z        
#>   <dbl> <list>    <list>   
#> 1     1 <chr [1]> <int [2]>
#> 2     2 <chr [2]> <dbl [1]>
df2 %>% unnest(y, z)
#> Warning: unnest() has a new interface. See ?unnest for details.
#> Try `df %>% unnest(c(y, z))`, with `mutate()` if needed
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>       x y         z
#>   <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1     1 a         1
#> 2     1 a         2
#> 3     2 b         3
#> 4     2 c         3
```
I am not sure if this was an intentional change to the behaviour of `nest()` or if it's a bug that should be reported to tidyr. If the first, then the last section in the "Many models" chapter should be adapted to reflect the new behaviour of the function.

title: Don't forget about slice() functions
description:
But the slice functions are super useful:

-   `slice_head()` and `slice_tail()` select the first or last rows in each group.

-   `slice_max()` and `slice_min()` select the rows in each group with highest or lowest values.

-   `slice_sample()` random selects rows from each group.

Each of these verbs takes either a n or prop argument depending on whether you want to select a fixed number of rows, or a number of rows proportional to the group size.

title: Move `master` branch to `main`

The `master` branch of this repository will soon be renamed to `main`, as part of a coordinated change across several GitHub organizations (including, but not limited to: [tidyverse](https://github.com/tidyverse), [r-lib](https://github.com/r-lib), [tidymodels](https://github.com/tidymodels), and [sol-eng](https://github.com/sol-eng)). title: Small change for clarity in 3.6
description:
Hi,

Currently there is this text "One line describes all of the points with a 4 value, one line describes all of the points with an f value, and one line describes all of the points with an r value." Perhaps it would be more immediately clear what this means by saying "One line describes all of the points that have a 4 value, one line describes all of the points that have an f value, and one line describes all of the points that have an r value."

The change from "with a" to "that have" avoids the momentary possibility of interpreting the text as saying that one line is describing the entirety of the values in the data-set through the 4 value. This is unlikely, due to the context, but it happened to me before realizing that wasn't the case.

A small change, I know. But hopefully helpful.

Best,
Gabriel

title: Automatic hyperlinking leads to wrong documentation
description:
There are a few cases where automatic hyperlinking leads to the wrong documentation. For example:

- In [1 Introduction](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/introduction.html#running-r-code), when talking about the prompt (`>`), the link leads to the documentation on [binary operators](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Comparison.html).
- In [3 Data visualisation](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/data-visualisation.html#common-problems), when talking about the `+` character in the console, the link leads to the documentation on [arithmetic operators](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Arithmetic.html).
- In [4 Workflow: basics](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/workflow-basics.html#exercises-7), `filter` links to [`stats::filter()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/filter.html) instead of [`dplyr::filter()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter.html).

title: Exercise 5.7.1.6 Seems like a bad question
description:
I have an issue with this question and it seems like bad methodology. The question reads as follows:

Look at each destination. Can you find flights that are suspiciously fast? (i.e. flights that represent a potential data entry error). Compute the air time of a flight relative to the shortest flight to that destination. Which flights were most delayed in the air?

My problem with this question is that you first identify these flights that are suspiciously fast, suggesting that they could be data entry errors, which would mean that they would be the shortest flight to that destination. Then afterwards you turn around and say to use these suspect flights to identify flights that are most delayed in the air. Seems to me like you should be comparing the flights with preferably the median, maybe the mean, to find the most delayed flights. Just a thought.

title: Exercise 23.4.5.3 is unclear
description:
I had a hard time making sense of exactly what this question was asking.

> Using the basic principles, convert the formulas in the following two models into functions. (Hint:  start by converting the categorical variable into 0-1 variables.)

> ```
> mod1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = sim3)
> mod2 <- lm(y ~ x1 * x2, data = sim3)
> ```

-  What are the expected inputs and outputs of the function? The most reasonable interpretation to me was to mimic the behavior of `model_matrix()` for the special cases of those formulas. But I could also interpret it as asking for a function to estimate the regression.
-  Should it be assumed that `x1` is continuous and `x2` is categorical? Or can `x1` and `x2` be anything. Since `sim3` is explicitly mentioned, I assume that is the case, but I'm not sure.

Some of these ambiguities are reasonable. Having to think through the complexity of how to handle formulas in generality and scoping it down to something feasible is a good lesson. However, the first question seems the most important. I think being more clear about the expected inputs and outputs of the function. Perhaps stating that the exercise is to write a function that does what `model_matrix()` does, but for these specific cases would make it more clear.

title: mapproj dependency
description:
In the 3.9.1 Exercises, #3 asks about `coord_map()` despite the fact that this function doesn't work without `mapproj` installed, a package that is only suggested in `ggplot2` documentation and isn't mentioned anywhere even in the optional packages for the book. And the book itself says it's not going to go into spatial mapping for lack of time.

It's an interesting question, but it seems like it should either be clarified somewhere that the mapping functionality of `coord_map()` depends on having `mapproj` installed or that the question should be taken out for being a little superfluous.

title: Exercise 5.4.3 is possibly obselete
description:
The question reads:

> What does the `one_of()` function do? Why might it be helpful in conjunction with this vector?

The need for `one_of()` is less obvious now that tidy eval exists.

Something like this,
```r
vars <- c("year", "month", "day", "dep_delay", "arr_delay")
select(flights, one_of(vars))
````
 can be replaced by this,
```r
select(flights, vars)
```
or this, to avoid ambiguity,
```r
select(flights, !!!vars)
```

title: dbplyr footnote or example or exercise
description:
After a year of teaching out of the r4ds book I have received some feedback from a number of students who took my class.  The main issues my students have had while interviewing for jobs is that they have been quizzed on SQL basics.  Having studied the dplyr they know a lot about how to wrangle data and do all of the things one can do with SQL, but they do not know the basic SQL commands SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, etc.

Having recently scrolled down on the main dbplyr page I was very happy to discover *show_query()*, *translate_sql()* and then I found the *RSQLite::dbGetQuery()* command. Using these function to introduce SQL while learning dplyr would be a nice way to learn some SQL.  And it might increase the opportunities of R users in the Data Science career path.

The most important being the *show_query()*.  Giving a footnote to the reader so they know of the existence of the dbplyr package would be great.  Suggesting that using dbplyr can be used to learn some basic relationships between dplyr and SQL.  

Giving a footnote, example, or an exercise would be great to point people in the right direction.

The r-bloggers recent [A Comprehensive Introduction to Working with Databases using R](https://www.r-bloggers.com/a-comprehensive-introduction-to-working-with-databases-using-r/) blog post from August 7 is an excellent reference beyond the [dbplyr](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/index.html) webpage.

I have not thought too much about which chapter or what page this should go on.  My first thought is at the end of Section 13.4.7 Other implementations.  Since there is a comparison of dplyr and SQL code given in the table there, this might be a good place to mention that dbplyr can be used to produce the SQL code from the dplyr code.

Here is one example using nycflights13 data.

```{r}
library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse, dbplyr, nycflights13, RSQLite)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

copy_to(con, flights)

flights2 <- tbl(con, "flights")

flights2_subset <- flights2 %>% 
  filter(month == 11 | month == 12)

flights2_subset %>% show_query()
```


```{r, echo=TRUE}
summary <- flights2 %>% 
  group_by(carrier) %>% 
  summarise(arr_delay_mean = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(arr_delay_mean))

summary %>% show_query()
```

description:
https://github.com/hadley/r4ds/blob/ce824d0a33149b34c7b1cacabf8636e132970592/strings.Rmd#L363

As I was writing lecture notes based on the "strings" chapter, I stumbled upon the exact same issue as described in this Reddit thread: https://www.reddit.com/r/rprogramming/comments/8oyy1a/stringr_str_view_repetition_at_most_n_times/

On my end, it looked like this. The intention was to show that there would be no match in this case. Instead, I get an error:

`str_view_all("Misery, Misery, Misery that’s what Lord and Miller have chosen", "(Misery, ){,3}")`

`Error in stri_locate_all_regex(string, pattern, omit_no_match = TRUE,  : 
  Error in {min,max} interval. (U_REGEX_BAD_INTERVAL)`

One of the answerers on Reddit explains:

> "`stringr` uses ICU regular expressions, which apparently do not have the `{,m}` notation - use the explicit `{n,m}`."

Since the `{,m}` "method" is presented as a viable option in the latest version of the book and I did not see an open issue related to this, I thought I'd mention it here.

Perhaps the error message when using `{,m}` is clear enough and the inclusion of `{,m}` in the book is intentional (in the sense that it discusses a valid regex, albeit one that does not work with `stingr`, and is judiciously not included in the examples of `stingr` applications)?

title: implict coercion in 16.4.2
description:
In one of the examples given in section 16.4.2 the following code is given. 

```
flights_dt <- flights_dt %>% 
  mutate(
    overnight = arr_time < dep_time,
    arr_time = arr_time + days(overnight * 1),
    sched_arr_time = sched_arr_time + days(overnight * 1)
  )
```

Since this book is geared toward novice-intermediate users of R it is my opinion that explicit coercion be preferred over implicit coercion. If implicit coercion is used it is also my opinion that it explicitly pointed out to the reader that implicated coercion was used.

the issue is with coercion that is occurring in this part of the code
```
overnight = arr_time < dep_time,
    days(overnight * 1),    
```

The variable "overnight" is of type logical and 1 is obviously of type numeric/double. R's coercion rules dictate that logical variables multiplied by a numeric variable results in the logical variable being automatically coerced into a numeric variable for binary evaluation.

I had someone ask me what was happening here and I had to explain it to them. My suggestion is to change this to 
```
overnight = arr_time < dep_time,
    days(as.numeric(overnight) * 1),    
```
which makes it apparent to novice readers what the intent is. You can either do that or add a simple inline comment such as 

```
overnight = arr_time < dep_time,
#binary arithmetic of logical variables against numeric variables will cause 
#the logical variable to be automatically coerced into a numeric type
#where FALSE = 0 and TRUE = 1.
    days(overnight * 1),    
```
"

This may make the code uglier but considering that this book was written for beginners I think it may be helpful to remind the readers to be aware of variable classes and coercion rules.

Thanks

description:
In 16.3.1, it says

"There’s an interesting pattern if we look at the average **departure** delay by minute within the hour. It looks like flights leaving in minutes 20-30 and 50-60 have much lower delays than the rest of the hour!"

In the following two plots, however, the parameter used is arr_delay, that is, arrival delay and not departure delay. The two plots (arr_delay vs dep_delay) look basically identical, so the punchline remains the same, but it is confusing.

title: Hint in Exercise 1 in 25.2.5
description:
Exercise 1 in 25.2.5 reads as follows: 

"A linear trend seems to be slightly too simple for the overall trend. Can you do better with a quadratic polynomial? How can you interpret the coefficients of the quadratic? (Hint you might want to transform year so that it has mean zero.)"

The hint is confusing. A quadratic polynomial has an additive term. Transforming year to have mean zero makes absolutely no difference, this kind of scaling is done by the polynomial.

title: 3.7 Statistical transformation stat_summary() example
description:
In the third example in section 3.7 of why you might explicitly set a stat by using the stat_summary() function, the book uses the code:

```
ggplot(data = diamonds) + 
  stat_summary(
    mapping = aes(x = cut, y = depth),
    fun.min = min,
    fun.max = max,
    fun = median
  )
```

However to get the same graph as in the book, one must use:

```
ggplot(data = diamonds) + 
  stat_summary(
    mapping = aes(x = cut, y = depth),
    fun.ymin = min,
    fun.ymax = max,
    fun.y = median
  )
```

title: Section 14.3.4 Repetition "{,m}: at most m" is not syntactically valid in regex
description:
In **chapter 14 Strings** > **Section 14.3.4 Repetition** it is mention that:

```
You can also specify the number of matches precisely:

- {,m}: at most m
```

However this syntaxis is not valid:

``` r
library(stringr)
x <- "1888 is the longest year in Roman numerals: MDCCCLXXXVIII"
str_view(x, "C{,1}")
#> Error in stri_locate_first_regex(string, pattern, opts_regex = opts(pattern)): Error in {min,max} interval. (U_REGEX_BAD_INTERVAL, context=`C{,1}`)
```
<sup>Created on 2021-03-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I want to know if this is a typo and if it is what would be the correct expression:

```
You can also specify the number of matches precisely:

- {1,m}: at most m

title: Section 3.8: The sentence "The values of hwy and displ are rounded so the points appear on a grid" can be misinterpreted
description:
In section 3.8, the sentence "The values of hwy and displ are rounded so the points appear on a grid and many points overlap each other." can be understood as that rounding happens at the time of plotting to make points fit on a grid. This interpretation is encouraged, in particular, by the fact that the previous section covers statistical transformations.

However, if I understand it correctly, the correct interpretation is that the hwy and displ values are already rounded in the mpg dataset, and that overplotting occurs because the coordinates of some points are, consequently, identical.

I think readability could be improved by rephrasing the sentence to remove any ambiguity in the interpretation.

title: optim doesn't use Newton-Raphson
description:
The *Model basics* section (23.1) says:

> But there’s a better way to tackle that problem: a numerical minimisation tool called Newton-Raphson search. The intuition of Newton-Raphson is pretty simple: you pick a starting point and look around for the steepest slope. You then ski down that slope a little way, and then repeat again and again, until you can’t go any lower. In R, we can do that with optim():

There are a few problems here.

- `optim` uses Nelder-Mead simplex by default
- it doesn't offer Newton-Raphson as an option (it does have some "quasi-Newton" algorithms such as BFGS)
- what's described here sounds more like *gradient descent* than N-R (although admittedly it could be a rough description of N-R).

title: 27.4.3 incorrectly describes data-frame printing
description:
27.4.3 says "R Markdown prints data frames and matrices as you’d see them in the console", using a code example of `mtcars[1:5, ]`. In fact, it produces a fairly attractive table by default:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/411495/112741657-3a66c700-8f4d-11eb-8f7d-af51ae981c51.png)

That is considerably different than the console output of the same command:
```
> mtcars[1:5, ]
                   mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
Mazda RX4         21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
Datsun 710        22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6  258 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8  360 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
```

It later mischaracterizes kable by suggesting that simply using `knitr::kable` causes "additional formatting". In fact, it causes *less* formatting:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/411495/112741670-641fee00-8f4d-11eb-9761-0f81b0953396.png)

It might be more correct to explain kable as something that can permit additional formatting options without suggesting that a unadorned use of kable will cause significant enhancements.

title: 14.2.2 Combining strings: Extra space is needed between "Good" and "morning"
description:
**The given syntax in the book:** (5th box under 14.2.2)

name <- "Hadley"
time_of_day <- "morning"
birthday <- FALSE 

str_c( 
  "Good", time_of_day, " ", name, 
  if (birthday)" and HAPPY BIRTHDAY", ".")

**Is written to result in:** 

"Good morning Hadley."

**But it really the output is:** 

"Goodmorning Hadley."

**Because there is no space indicated between "Good" and "morning"  **

**Change code to:**

str_c( 
  "Good",  " ", time_of_day, " ", name, 
  if (birthday)" and HAPPY BIRTHDAY", ".")

title: "Cursor" character can be selected in workflow-scripts.
description:
In `workflow-scripts.Rmd` the character █ is used to represent the cursor.  If you copy the code sample that character also gets copied.  This led to a confused student today:

```.R
not_cancelled <- flights %>% 
  filter(!is.na(dep_delay)█, !is.na(arr_delay))
```

Some browsers support `user-selected: none` CSS style that could prevent that character from being selected.  Unfortunately, as far as I can tell, you would have to teach pandoc how to do this, so it would require a lot of effort, for small gain.  I put this here in case I am mistaken and there is an easy post processing step that could make the small change.

title: 5.5.2 usefulness of time comparison exercise
description:
I might be missing something, but it seems that the second exercise in 5.5.2 might be confusing as:

- `dep_time` and `arr_time` use the local time-zone, and
- `air_time` is almost never equivalent to `arr_time - dep_time` even when converted to minutes and corrected for time-zones (not sure why?).

Sorry if I am missing something obvious.

title: Typo in Fig 3.1: shapes
description:
In [Fig 3.1](http://r4ds.had.co.nz/data-visualisation.html#fig:shapes), which is at the end of [section 3.3: Aesthetic Mappings](http://r4ds.had.co.nz/data-visualisation.html#aesthetic-mappings), the shapes are oddly layed out by number (counting by column it goes: 0, 1, 2, 5, 3, 4, 6, 7...). 

Perhaps as a result of this, there are two shapes missing in the description of the interaction of the shape, colour and fill aesthetics.

> The hollow shapes (0-14) have a border determined by `colour`; the solid shapes (15-18) are filled with `colour`; the filled shapes (21-24) have a border of `colour`and are filled with `fill`.

19 and 20 should both be in the solid shapes category.

To fix the typo, the text could read:

> The hollow shapes (0-14) have a border determined by `colour`; the solid shapes (15-20) are filled with `colour`; the filled shapes (21-24) have a border of `colour`and are filled with `fill`.

I expect fixing the image in the figure (with a better layout of the shapes by number) would be a lower priority, but the text fix could occur by itself and solve the typo.

After reading the "Exploratory Data Analysis" chapter I realised that 4 datasets (diamonds, mpg, faithful and flights) had been used in that chapter alone! title: ## 5.2.2 Logical operators: Incorrect description of `filter(flights, month == 11 | 12)`
description:
While teaching Data Science and Statistics with RStudio at the University of the Faroe Islands, I noticed this issue. 

In 5.2.2 Logical operators the online textbook (http://r4ds.had.co.nz/) claims:

## 5.2.2 Logical operators

"The order of operations doesn’t work like English. You can’t write `filter(flights, month == 11 | 12)`, which you might literally translate into “finds all flights that departed in November or December. In a numeric context (like here), `TRUE` becomes one, so this finds all flights in January, not November or December. This is quite confusing!”. 

This sentence is incorrect: ", so this finds all flights in January, not November or December. This is quite confusing!".

The code `filter(flights, month == 11 | 12)` does not only find the flights in January, since filter(flights, month == 11 | 12) does not filter flights, but simply returns flights due to the always-TRUE condition.

```{r}

# the intended filter
filter(flights, month == 11 | month == 12)

# this code does not filter the data (all months will be included)
filter(flights, month == 11 | 12)

```
best regards
Hannes Gislason

I'm submitting this issue wearing my hat as Education Fellow at Creative Commons. I noticed today that you're using a Creative Commons license with the ND condition (CC BY-NC-ND) for R4DS. I know that you actively encourage people to clone the repo, make changes, and submit PRs based on those changes. On its face it would seem that cloning a repo, making changes to its content, and sharing that changed content - when that content is ND licensed - would be a violation of the license. Is this something you've considered? I'd be happy to jump on a Skype or similar to discuss if that would be helpful.

Even though I know an Issue isn't the best venue, please let me say I'm a huge fan of your work. R4DS and the Tidyverse have totally changed my professional life for the better.

title: Is the syntax highlighting theme available in RStudio?
description:
This question is acutally about RStudio, not really about the book, but I wanted to post here because posts in RStudio support often have no response for long time.

I found the syntax highlighting theme for code in book very informative. Once the code in book was copied to RStudio, they become rather dull with same color for almost everything. Two very helpful differences are the known library function names (bold green) and the function parameter assignments (dark red).

The theme in book seemed to be implemented by customized CSS, but there should be no difficulty to implement similar effect in RStudio. I searched RStudio support and found several similar requests dated as early as 2013.

I submitted [a feature request in RStudio support](https://support.rstudio.com/hc/en-us/community/posts/211643088-syntax-highlighting-for-known-function-names-parameter-names)

title: Single character class for regex metacharacters
description:
Re: the chapter on strings and how to include a literal metacharacter in the string representation of the regular expression.

It might be worth mentioning that a character class with that single character is an alternative to all the backslashes for many of the metacharacters. I think the resulting regex is more readable. I wish I remembered this more often myself!

Tacking this on at the end of an existing example:

``` r
# To create the regular expression, we need \\
dot <- "\\."

# But the expression itself only contains one:
writeLines(dot)
#> \.

# And this tells R to look for an explicit .
stringr::str_view(c("abc", "a.c", "bef"), "a\\.c")

# And so does this
stringr::str_view(c("abc", "a.c", "bef"), "a[.]c")
```

Preliminary fact collecting

👍 metacharacters for which this works: `$` `.` `|` `?` `*` `+` `(` `)` `[` `{` 

👎 for which this does not work, i.e. they have special meaning inside a character class: `]` `\` `^` `-`

title: suggested change in 14.4.1
description:
When using str_detect() to match a pattern and filter a tibble, you filter using "words," the vector, while it should be "word," the column name. This would ensure consistency should "words" change.

`df <- tibble(
    word = words,
    i = seq_along(word)
)`

# original:
`df %>%
    filter(str_detect(words, "x$"))`

# change to:
`df %>% 
    filter(str_detect(word, "x$"))`
